html:
The Araweté, who call themselves Bïde ("human beings"), are a Tupi-Guarani speaking people of the Xingu River basin in Pará, Brazil. They farm forest gardens of maize and manioc and hunt.

They lived in the upper Bacajá area until attacks by the Kayapó and others drove them toward the Ipixuna River. They first had peaceful contact with Brazilian government agents in 1976, and many died of disease in the following years. The anthropologist Eduardo Viveiros de Castro made their beliefs well known: in Araweté thought the dead are eaten by gods in the sky and so become gods themselves. The Belo Monte dam on the Xingu, built in the 2010s, brought new pressure on their land. Their neighbours include the Asurini of the Xingu.
